en: Immediately after the *argha* offering, this procedure for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is taught:

the wise one, having taken possession of a plot of ground that is well-prepared, [should adorn it] with canvas curtains, canopies, and the like, as well as garlands, hanging wreaths, chowries, and so forth. [4.1]
With fragrant perfumes and incense, and with lamps;
with jasmine, campaka, saugandhika, nāgakesara, and kesara flowers;
with pūthikā, mallikā, mlāna, pāṭala, kamala, and utpala lotuses.
Adorned with various garments such as *karṇikāra* flowers and the like,
it is decorated outside with banners, flags, and the like, and graced by the *kadalī* tree;
it is further embellished by the sounds of *kāhāla* and conch shells, and by various musical instruments.
A place smeared with fragrant unguents and strewn with flowers on all sides—
on such a spot as this one should arrange the maṇḍala,
having warded off obstacles by means of the bali-mantras and other rites.
Even though phenomena are unarisen and devoid of middle or extremes,

what obstacle could there be in the investigation of their practice, and who could be harmed? [4.7] It is through ignorance of intrinsic nature that truth is subverted, not by intrinsic nature itself.
The warding off of obstacles for sentient beings of weak, middling, and other capacities has been explained.
Even though phenomena are unarisen and devoid of middle or extremes,
the construction of the mandala is accomplished through yoga with one’s own tutelary deity.
Then, with divine powder, or else with medium-quality powder,
or with powders made of the five precious gems, or even with rice and so forth,
the wise one should fashion the maṇḍala according to his means. [4.10]
In the center of the maṇḍala house, accompanied by four disciples,
having offered water for honor and water for the feet and so forth, and having attained meditative absorption,
he is surrounded by other disciples standing in the four directions who hold bells and vajras.

And by those who have formed the maṇḍala in the forms of Vairocana and the others, with verses, the Maṇḍalācārya—who has attained supreme joy—should be requested. [4.12] % *anne* means "furthermore"; *paramaubilyatām* means "supreme joy."
In this regard, there is a verse: || o ||
Teach the supreme maṇḍala, which is quiescent and belongs to all Tathāgatas, the abode of all Tathāgatas, and the foremost selflessness of all phenomena. [4.13] Teach.
Perfectly endowed with all marks and free from all non-marks,
speak of the supreme maṇḍala, the foremost body of Samantabhadra,
which arises from the excellence of the peaceful dharmas and purifies the conduct of primordial wisdom. [4.14]
O Charioteer of the Maṇḍala of Sound, the supreme speech of Samantabhadra!
O Charioteer of the Maṇḍala of Sound, the supreme mind of Samantabhadra—the great mind of all sentient beings, pure and naturally stainless! [4.15–4.16]

Having heard the request, the Master— having resolved the obstacles against the host of afflictions, being enraged toward the afflictions that pervade the three worlds— raised the mandala in the expanse of the sky with this verse: [4.17]
The mantra called a *gāthā*: Oṃ vajra tiṣṭha.
Having established that [mantra] within the expanse of space, with a face radiating light;
His eyes are like the moon and sun with the sound of *maṭkāra*, and his forest of stars is the syllable *hūṃ*.
Possessing great splendor like the fire at the end of an eon, he is intent on brandishing the vajra.
With masses of light-rays from the strike of his feet, which possess a radiance equal to the fire of a vajra— [4.18–4.19]
Seeing the wicked ones fled from all sides there in that pure place,
[the Teacher] beheld their great nourishment through the cool masses of light rays, saturated with nectar, which had issued forth from the syllable Oṃ,
as they were reunited with their own side.
Having performed the act of appeasement in that place, the supreme knower of mantras,
full of vajra-pride, should move gracefully from the northeastern direction,
properly circling with vajra-steps together with his principal disciples. [4.21–4.22]
Having assumed an even posture and joined his palms above his head, the yogin stands facing the east and pays homage to the Tathāgatas. [4.23]
Bowing with palms joined at the crown of the head and at the heart through the union of the lotuses,
one should whirl them in all directions and then form the vajra-fist.
Having indeed split the fist into two parts, one should perform the binding of the universal projection.
Skilled in dancing with vajra-steps through the conjunctions of clapping hands,

one should perceive the earth from the surface down to the subterranean realm as consisting of universal vajras, and even as consisting of fire by means of the masses of light rays produced from the feet. [4.25–4.26]
Having assumed the ocean-shaking posture (*sāgarāndolaka*), one should perform the serpent-throwing gesture (*nāgākṣepa*).
Having formed the "swarm of bees" (*bhramarījāla*) mudrā, one should place the heart-mantra upon the *kālāgni*.
Then, having assumed the *ālīḍha* stance, one dances with the *pratyālīḍha* stance.
Then, having performed the *āli* and *kāli* gestures five times in the manner of the lotus-spiral (*kamalāvarta*),
the wise practitioner, making a grand display with the sound of the bell and holding the vajra in his hand with wonder,
should then perform the dance through expressive gesture (*abhinaya*).
Then, having performed the brandishing of the spear, one should display the brandishing of the bow;
moreover, by means of the gesture of a garland of flowers, one should cause the touching of the secret place.
In that [state], the skillful one, equal to the disciple, [should act] with terrible sounds of the syllable *hūṃ*.
One should cause the wicked inhabitants of that place to utter these words, reciting this mantra-phrase which was spoken by the Buddha:
"May those who are the lords of this place depart! [4.31]
On this very spot of earth, for the sake of fulfilling the awakening of such-and-such a disciple, a Vajrin, and for the sake of the wisdom of living beings,
I shall draw the mandala of the glorious Vajradhara.
"Therefore, by this word of mine, depart quickly!
And for whoever does not depart from here, Vajradhara himself [will deal with them]. [4.34]
Then, with a vajra blazing from the syllable *hūṃ* and set ablaze,
the best of those who know mantras, filled with wrath, should split open the head.
Reciting this mantra in such a manner, the practitioner should circumambulate three times to the right.
With these fifteen [elements], one who is composed should perform the dance again;
otherwise, the congregations will perish and fall apart.
Thus it is said in the *Rativajra*:
With rays arising from the sun, as if produced by the fires at the end of an aeon.
[One should think: "By whom have they been shaken up? By whom have they been caused to tremble? One should imagine the wicked fleeing here and there, being consumed by fire. [4.37]
From the *Piṇḍīkrama*:
"Then, one should point out eight dilapidated wells in the eight directions;
[there are] eight dilapidated wells in the [cardinal] directions."
Then, bearing the wrathful *hūṃ* syllable from the *hūṃ* syllable in one’s own heart,
[one draws forth] the fierce ones, such as Yamāntaka and the rest, who have been summoned by the sounds of the *hūṃ* syllables.
Having emanated the Lord Ṭakkirāja from the mantra *Ṭakki hūṃ*,
one should draw them in with that noose and goads at their throats;
then, having drawn in all the hosts of obstructors by means of the Lord of Obstructors, [one should proceed].
The best of mantra-practitioners should cast those stakes made of *khadira* wood— which possess the very form of Vajrasattva— into the previously mentioned wells within the food. [4.41]
Then [he struck] those stakes known as Anantavijaya, Meghanāda,
and Mahodara.
Having established the five *kīlas* of the nature of the five Buddhas— namely, the one called Jayākhya—
in the center, and having placed the others in the intermediate directions in their proper order.

The wise one, having fashioned [the implements] in the form of vajras known as the "many-pointed" (*anekasūka*), extremely sharp and measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*) according to the measure of a Jina,
should then fashion the obstructors above them in the form of Vighnāntaka.

In their respective directions, by means of these [deities] who hold thunderbolt-bows and arrows, and through this mantra consisting of fierce syllables such as *hūṃ* and so forth, the practitioner of yoga [should act]:

*Oṃ gha gha ghātaya 2 sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ | kīlaya 2 sarvapāpān phaṭ hūṃ 3 vajrakīla vajradharo ājñāpayati sarvavighnānāṃ kāyavākcittavajraṃ kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ |* [Oṃ gha gha slay, slay all evil ones, phaṭ! Stake, stake all sins, phaṭ! Hūṃ 3! O Vajrakīla, Vajradhara commands: stake the vajra-body, speech, and mind of all obstructors, hūṃ phaṭ!]
Having beheld the eight fierce Vighnas and Vināyakas, as formidable as the sun, together with their retinues, one should contemplate emptiness for the sake of destroying them at birth.
Then, having projected Hayagrīva outside the peaked pavilion, [one should proceed].
One should visualize them as having the form of a cage of missiles through transformation;
then, one should again visualize [the goddess] arisen from the syllable Hrīḥ, pervading the entire sky.
And so it is said in the *Vajraśikhara*:
"When the practitioner of mantra is established in the visualization (*kalpanā*), he should purify the grounds."
O Lord of Secrets, that ground upon which a mantra-practitioner who has abandoned the *bodhicitta* stands does not become purified.
The mantra-practitioner, reciting the *vajrasattva*, should gaze with the *vajra-vision*.
Even if it is defective, the ground portion of the mandala is purified.
[4.49] The procedure for purifying the ground. [fleuron]

Having sat down again, the practitioner, placing his right knee upon the ground and taking up incense, should address the Earth deity: "O Earth, deity of food! [4.50] % [He should address the Earth deity as follows: "O Earth, deity of food!"
O Goddess, you are the witness for all the Buddhas who protect beings, regarding the specificities of the methods of conduct and the stages and perfections.
Just as the army of Māra was defeated by the excellent ones, such as the Lion of the Śākyas; [4.51]
"Having thus conquered the host of Māra, I shall draw the mandala," having recited this, he should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*).
Then, having smeared the ground of the mandala with true sandalwood and other substances, [he should proceed].
Beginning with the arrangement of flowers on the ground, one should draw the thirty-two deities and nineteen [other] locations using the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Having mentally drawn the mandala situated in the sky and caused it to enter [the disciple],
one should perform the binding of the boundary and so forth with the fivefold offering. [4.54]
Immovable and possessing the nature of ultimate reality, their very essence is compassion; they remove the suffering of the world.
Bestowing all supreme accomplishments without exception, possessing stainless, immovable, and peerless supreme qualities.
They are considered pure and immovable;
there exists no equality with them in the sky, not even in a minute particle of a fraction of their qualities, for they are boundless.
[They are] those who bestow the supreme accomplishment of the manifest realm of sentient beings, who are beyond comparison, and whose accomplishments are without limit. [4.56]

May the Protectors— who abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) that is cessation within the fire of equanimity, who delight in bestowing the supreme boon at the proper time, and who are unstained by the impurities of the three realms of existence— grant them to me. Thus,
one should introduce [the ritual] with these verses of praise spoken during the Three Samayas.
[Then] the praise with the verses spoken by the Mother;
the presentation of the five nectars and so forth; the bell and the incense ladle;
having touched the ground with the knees and gazed toward the expanse of the sky. [4.58+]
He said, "O Blessed One, O Akṣobhya, King of Vidyās, homage be to you!
I wish to write down the name of the mandala whose nature is compassion, for the sake of showing favor to disciples and for the worship of you all. [4.59+]
O Blessed One, you ought to grant me that one favor!
May the Buddhas— who bestow the purpose of the wheel of activity for the world— take heed of me,
as well as the Bodhisattvas established in the fruit and whatever other mantra-deities there may be.
The world-protectors are likewise such beings, governed by the Perfectly Complete Enlightenment;
all those who possess the vajra-eye delight in the teaching.
I, the Vajra-holder named so-and-so, am the maṇḍala arising from Akṣobhya.
I shall write this for the accomplishment of the world, according to my capacity and understanding. Out of compassion, may you and your disciples all together grant your presence within this mandala.
Thus one should perform the consecration in three ways.
This is the ritual procedure for the consecration.
Furthermore, having smeared the ground of the mandala all around with fragrance,
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with powders of white, yellow, and other colors.
Having placed in its center the flask named "all-purpose" (sārvakarmika), [one should proceed].
One should place a thread made of five colors upon the eastern lotus petal;
the bell should be placed on the northern petal, and the supreme vajra on the southern one.

One should place a conch filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) upon the western petal. With a concentrated mind, the practitioner, having donned the armor of the factors of enlightenment through the visualization of his own tutelary deity, should deposit colored powders in the vicinity of the lotus.
One should offer the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) along with flowers, incense, and so forth, together with food offerings and ritual oblations;
having fully manifested the being within the vase, possessing a radiance equal to the whiteness of the moon.
One should project the left hand with a gracefully swinging bell and the right hand holding a vajra;
the yogin should form the mudrā of the khaṭvāṅga empowered by mantra.
Then, having formed two fists, the two little fingers should be placed at the position of the breasts.
Raising the little fingers and bending them, one should display this mudrā at the heart.
[4.71+] Mudrā. Mantra: oṃ āḥ svāhā.
One should touch it with the tip of the vajra and recite the mantra eight hundred times.
Having recited the seed-syllable consisting of the five Buddhas, one should stretch out the thread:
OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ SVĀHĀ.
Alternatively, there may be the sprinkling of powders with the *kūṭabīja*:
OṂ SMRYUṂ SVĀHĀ.
Having made offerings of various oblations to the cardinal and intermediate directions and the eight islands,
one who is well-composed should instruct the artisan on the work of the thread.
Having gathered everything together, one should then place the water-pots to the south.
Having smeared it with sandalwood and other substances, one should offer a sacrificial oblation there. Thus ends the procedure for the consecration of the ground.
For it has been said:
"In all undertakings of works, wherever they may be, one should offer a bali at the beginning and at the end for the pacification of all obstacles. [4.76+]

One who knows the ritual procedures should offer the bali-oblation based on the *Pīṭhatantras*, or that which is taught in other tantras; or else, one should offer the bali according to the rite of the *Samāja*.
(4.77+) *Pīṭhatantra* refers to the *Catuṣpīṭha*.
Having again placed all the curd-rice and other offerings before him,
one should manifest them through the rite of the four seats (catuṣpīṭha) as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
assuming white and other colors according to the three principles (tritattva) taught in that particular tantra.
[How does one perform] the three principles (tattva) as taught in the *Anuttaratantra*? With the seed-syllables *haḥ*, *hoḥ*, and *hrīḥ*, written with *oṃ svāhā* at the beginning and end:
the syllable *haḥ* removes color, and the syllable *hoḥ* destroys fragrance.
The syllable *hrīḥ* is the destroyer of vigor; its function is now described.
(4.80+) Is the sequence [of these] being prescribed here?

Having properly presided over all things in a threefold manner by means of the three principles (*tritattva*), the practitioner of yoga, having firmly formed the *vajrāñjali* mudrā at the region of the heart, recites:
*Oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham*. (4.81+)
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure like a vajra; I am pure like a vajra.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.
Having performed the *kamalāvartana* gesture, one should place the right hand upon a lotus;
releasing the *vajra* in the left, one should display the *mahāmudrā*.
Lifting up the food: Oṃ haḥ hoḥ hrīḥ svāhā.
This is the mantra for the consecration of the mudrā.

The syllable *haḥ* is Padmanṛtyeśa, possessing a form of golden color; this *hoḥ* syllable, whose nature is scented water, is considered to be Rocana. The syllable *hrīḥ* is Rasavajrā; he himself is the Lord Vajrapāṇi.
Furthermore, those who know meditation should meditate upon the three deities beginning with the three *tattvas*.
On the left, in the center of the moon-syllable *aṃ*, is that tenfold nectar; therein is that very seed-syllable.
Having drawn [the mandala] with the light of that seed-syllable, the expanse of the sky becomes a mandala named Meru;
having churned it like the ocean by means of the right ring finger according to the procedure for churning, all of that indeed—
Having obtained that triangle, the yogin should draw it upon the ground and perform the libation and other rites with it.
Having again fashioned a square mandala, he should worship it with flowers, incense, and so forth.
One should present the collection of offerings, such as curd-rice and so forth, to the assembly of deities.
Having recited the great mantra of summoning (*ākṛṣṭi*) while being intent upon its corresponding mudrā, one should likewise proceed.
Having formed two vajra-fists joined back-to-back,
with the earth-canopy lotus-encirclement, one raises the white *arocana*;
by the contraction of the white [fist], one should summon the gods from the eastern quarter.
By means of the application of mudrās, mantras, and so forth, the practitioner should offer the bali-oblation. [4.88+]

Oṃ patuli padmapatuli hūṃ hūṃ jaḥ svāhā. With the left hand holding a moon-vessel and the right hand in the solar fist, one should carefully raise the white [deity] by means of the graceful posture (lalitākṣepa).

Oṃ! O summoner, great summoner, summoner of the *pretas*, you whose face is the accomplishment of the sun and moon, Yaya [or Maya?], Aparājitā, Somarājī, Goddess Umā, Gaṅgā of beautiful form, Tārāsaṃgrahā, Lord of all the Gaṇas, Kārtika, Śrī Śaśidevī, Agala, Pagala, King of the Asuras and Suras, Pukkasi, Mahāpukkasi: Haṃ Hoḥ! Summon, summon! For the sake of meditative absorption, Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Jaḥ Svāhā!
Thereafter, with the previous mudrā: Oṃ bhakṣa 2 samādhipati hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Having satisfied [the deity] with this mantra, one should dismiss [them] with three *śocis* oblations.
This is the *devabali*.
At the location of the northern gate, standing on the tip of his foot,
with a hand ringing a vajra-bell, he brandishes the vajra like the sun.
There, white flowers and the like, along with milk-rice, constitute the food offering (*naivedya*).
Having firmly formed the "moon-fist" (*candramuṣṭi*) mudrā, one raises the "earth-umbrella" (*bhūcchatra*) gesture.
Then, extending the "sun-hand" (*sūryapāṇi*), one forms a hood (*phaṇā*) above it.
The invocation of the nāgas is prescribed by means of the very same mantra mentioned previously; this is the mantra for the bali offering.

Oṃ! Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Kuliśapāla, Devati, Mahādevati, Somaśikhi, Mahāśikhi, Daṇḍadhara, Mahādaṇḍadhara, Apalāṅgalunda, Nanda, Upananda, Sāgara, Mahāsāgara, Tapta, Mahātaptta, Śrīkānti, Mahākānti, Ratnakānti, Surūpa, Mahāsurūpa, Bhadrāhika, Mahodara, Śili, Mahāśili—Oṃ! Come, come! To the lord of the great nāgas, all of you! Bhūr bhuvaḥ phaṭ svāhā!
The dismissal is as before.
The Nāga-offering. [Fleuron]

Relying on the western part, one should create a red mandala with perfumes of red, yellow, and other colors, as well as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). Having invoked the yakṣas and yakṣiṇīs by means of the "mandala-projection" step, [one should proceed].
With the previously mentioned mantra and mudrā, the adept should offer the yakṣa-bali.
The mantra is as follows: [4.95+] mantraḥ.

Oṃ! Māṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Subhadra, Jayabhadra, Nandī, Kīla, Mahākīla, Padmaśikhara, Śaṅkhaśikhara, Nabha, Mahānabha, Bhedani, Chedani, Pūraṇi, Dhanādhanamūdhana, Surūpa, Keli, Mahākeli, Hasati, Krīḍitavikṣepa, Supriya, Surūpā, Kānti! By this command of the Vajradhara, O Yakṣas and Yakṣiṇīs, come forth, come forth! Enter, enter! Great entry! Eat, O beloved one, in the midst of the Yoginīs! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā!
Having firmly pressed both fists together against the region of the heart,
one who is compassionate should offer an oblation for the sake of pleasing the yakṣas;
the dismissal is performed with a snap of the fingers directed toward the east.
Then, as before, with three snaps of the fingers, the *yakṣa* offering is made. [Fleuron]
Having stepped forward with the vajra-step and taken recourse at the southern gate,
one should draw a triangular maṇḍala using substances such as blood and marrow,
along with red flowers, incense, dried fish, and meat.

One should offer various kinds of foods and edibles, such as onions, sesame paste, and the five types of *kulmāṣa* (half-cooked grains), along with the five nectars (*amṛta*), to the Guardian of the Field (*kṣetrapāla*). Having invoked the spirits (*bhūta*) who bestow prosperity by means of the previously mentioned mantras and mudrās, one should present these offerings.
Having announced it with the sounds of drums and a terrifying proclamation in triple rhythm,
the skillful practitioner who knows the ritual procedure and holds the bell and vajra should offer the bali.
The mantra for the bali offering. [Fleuron]
Under a solitary tree, or in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a cave or a grotto—
especially near a village, on a path, in a field, or in an empty house.
In a vessel placed on the ground, and especially in the house of the Mother (Mātṛgṛha),
one should rely upon Kṛṣṇa, Rudra, Mahārudra, and Devadatta;
as well as Kṛṣṇakarālī, Bībhatsī, Nandātītā, and Vināyikā.
Cāmuṇḍā, Ghorabībhatsī, and Umādevī are the Mothers;
likewise Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā;
as well as Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, and Sthūlakālī the Yoginī.
Indrī, Candrī, Ghorī, Daṃṣṭrī, Lampākī, Tridaśeśvarī;
Kāmbojī, Dīpinī, and the Yoginī residing in the village who drinks [blood],
Ghorarūpā, Mahārūpā, Daṃṣṭrārūpā, and Karālinī.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, holding a khaṭvāṅga and possessing great supernatural power (*maharddhika*),
with a sword and an axe in her hands, and likewise a vajra, a bow, and a thunderbolt in her hand—
she is the accomplisher (*sādhaka*) of all activities through the vajra of great bliss.
The Lord, the sovereign of the great king of the yoga-maṇḍala,
likewise [is] the emanation of the stainless yoga, the great body of the Tathāgata.
This is the command of the Vajra-holder for all beings:
Oṃ kka kka ḍhaṇa ba bba bandhana kha khkha khādana hana 2 pātaya 2 sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ 2 phaṭ jaḥ svāhā.
Filling the mouth with nectar (*amṛta*), one should contemplate in accordance with the ritual action. The Yogas and Yoginīs should be visualized; thus, all rites are accomplished. [4.109+]
Having formed two vajra-fists joined back-to-back,
there is Bhūcandā; Padmaveṣṭā is white, as is Śvetārocanaśṛṅkhalā.
Oṃ tiṣṭha hūṃ bhakṣa bhakṣa jaḥ phaṭ svāhā.
To the south is the bali offering for the Kṣetrapāla.
Then one should perform the song: "The drum resounds; O Bhavānī, the limbs are joined to the limbs. Grant me the splendor of the host of Gaṇas, O Unadorned One! Hūṃ hūṃ! [4.111+]
Then, having sounded the bell with auspicious songs according to one's desire,
and having firmly formed the vajra-añjali mudrā, one should hold it at the location of the heart;
and having made aspirations for the enlightenment of all sentient beings.
Having firmly formed the vajra-fist with the left hand, one should place it at the heart;
having extended the right hand and placed it on the ground, one should release it. Oṃ ātma tiṣṭha siddha svāhā.
Those beginning with the gods who have been brought for the sake of the bali-offering by means of mantra and mudrā— brought for the sake of the bali-offering,
they stand possessing their own full maturation and assuming their characteristic forms and weapons.
All [the deities] should be meditated upon in brief as assuming their own forms and endowed with lower garments, where the best of those who know the four seats (catuṣpīṭha) [is worshipped].
This is the bali offering as taught in the Pīṭhatantra.
Alternatively, one should offer the bali with the verses taught in the Subāhu-tantra.

In that regard, having divided the previously mentioned foods, edibles, and so forth into two portions, one should recite this verse for the purpose of worshipping the planets over one of the portions.

Gods, asuras, all serpents, siddhas, tārkṣyas, suparṇas, and kaṭapūtanas; gandharvas, yakṣas, and whatever classes of grahas dwell upon the earth, whether they be divine or otherwise— I, having placed one knee upon the surface of the earth and with palms joined in reverence, address them.
Having heard this, may they come here together with their sons, wives, and hosts of servants for the sake of showing grace.
[4.117+] Those beings who dwell upon the summit of Meru, those in the Nandana grove, and those in the abode of the gods;
those on Mount Udaya, in the residence of the Sun, and all those who dwell upon every mountain—[4.118+]
Those who have made their dwellings in all rivers and at their confluences, even in the abodes of jewels;
in ponds, lakes, pools, wells, embankments, and waterfalls;
those who are in village hamlets or in city groves, or those who dwell in military outposts or in temples.
Those elephants who dwell in monasteries, shrines, guest-houses, hermitages, alms-halls, and assembly halls;
those who reside in the painted chambers of kings, on carriage-roads, in streets, and at crossroads;
and those who live in great cremation grounds and vast forests inhabited by lions, elephants, and bears.

Those who dwell in terrible great forests and have made their homes on divine islands; those who reside joyfully and with serene minds upon Mount Meru or in cremation grounds, adorned with garlands, perfumes, and wreaths—
may they, whoever they may be, receive, enjoy, and drink with devotion the incense, the offering, and the ritual of lamps.
And may they enjoy this fruitful rite!
Having performed the worship of the planetary deities (grahas) in this manner, one should recite this verse for the purpose of worshipping the deities of the directions in the subsequent section.
May the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrī) in the eastern quarter, together with the hosts of spirits, accept this distinguished offering;
as well as Agni, Yama, Nairṛti, the Lord of Beings (Bhūpati), the Lord of Waters (Apāmpati), Vāyu, and the Lord of Wealth (Dhanādhipa);
the Lord of Spirits (Bhūtādhipati) in the northeast, the gods, and above, the Moon, the Sun, and the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
May the gods on all sides of the earth, and the nāgas who support the world, together with the hosts of guhyakas;
having each been individually invited in their respective directions,
may they accept [this offering], being satisfied, along with their forces, their armies, and accompanied by their sons, friends, and kinsmen.
"May they enjoy this incense, the offering, and the presentation of flowers; may they smell, taste, and drink this.
May they accept this ritual act as fruitful.
Thus one should exit. Om.
Now the laying out of the lines is described.

Why is this in larger letters? But the teacher, having reached a firm decision, should himself cause the descent of the special thread-markings to be performed in due order, accompanied by a pure assembly of disciples. [4.128+]
The wise one should trace the lines with a new, well-prepared, well-proportioned, and beautiful thread, through union with his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
Having placed the central point upon that ground, he should do so in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
With no lines omitted or crooked, accompanied by the sound of the syllable *hūṃ*,
the disciple faces west while the master likewise faces east;
with the *vajra* concentration, they should cast down the Brahma-thread.
[How does one perform] the Vajrasūtra-samādhi?
Taking the thread with the stylus, from the south toward the north;
[how does one use] the stylus?
One should draw two lines toward each direction, forming a "fish-tail" (matsyapucchaka) junction. When the directions are established,
the second Brahma-line is situated between the south and the north.
The Guru performs [the rite] with the disciples by means of a clockwise rotation. Among the disciples,
one who possesses two measures has two threads, while one who possesses one measure has six threads.
In the case of four *mātrās* and two *sūtras*, the mandala should indeed be thus;
the measure for the five lines of the *dhāraṇī* should be two *mātrās*.
The jeweled band (*ratnapaṭṭī*) is one *mātrā*, while the necklace (*hāra*) and half-necklace (*ardhahāra*) are two *mātrās* each.
The jeweled band and the *bakulī* are each one *mātrā*.
There should be fifteen threads on each side of the two Brahma-threads.
One should properly drop a thread from the southeast corner situated in fire and wind;
the two [threads] situated in the southwest and northeast corners should drop the second [thread].
With the measurement of one central square, there are three lines within the eight squares.
The wise one should erase each [line] externally according to the sequence of the stabilizing lines.
At the junction of the two Brahmās and in the vicinity of the Lord of the Wheel,
that very same thread [is drawn] through the four square-sections of the Buddhas.

Likewise, the wise one should then determine the mutual distance between those goddesses' squares; from there, in the intermediate directions, he should fashion pillars adorned with squares marked by measures,
where this circular area consists of fourteen measures.

Outside of that is a circle one *mātrā* wide, and outside of that is a garland of vajras. The panel for the deities is raised up, and there is no line anywhere else. Outside of that is the panel for the deities, measuring four *mātrās*.

In the corners are Rūpavajrā and the others; on the sides of the eastern and other doors are Brāhmaṇī and the wrathful deities (krodhas). Having erased the four lines, then two by two horizontal lines should be struck out from the side of Brahmā.
The square consisting of the mere enclosure has indeed a base of five lines.
At the door of the two wing-projections (*pakṣa-niryūha*), on the outside, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, there should be five lines beyond that; and the *kapola* is situated within.
The pillar (*stambha*) should be seven *mātrās* in height; the triple-vajra border (*añcala*) is three units.

The spokes (*ārā*) rest upon the lines (*rekhā*), as does the water-channel (*vāriṇī*). There are two types of *mātṛkā*. The jeweled band (*ratnapaṭṭī*) consists of one *mātrikā*; the necklace (*hāra*) and half-necklace (*ardhahāra*) consist of two *mātrās*; and the jeweled *bakulī* consists of one *mātrikā*.
At the base of the door-jambs, there is a matrix of vajra-gems,
each measuring four units; furthermore, in the outer enclosure outside the vases,
from Kṣitigarbha onwards, there shall be the Saṃāja-maṇḍala.
Outside is the common *āsāra* (enclosure), which is considered to be the *mātṛkā* situated on the pillar. Outside of that, the *bakulī*, *ratna*, and *khura* are each one *mātrā* in height;
they occupy eighteen parts above and fourteen parts on the sides.
The jeweled fillet (*ratnapaṭṭī*) and the *bakulikā* should each be one sixteenth part;

the hoof-plate (*khurāpaṭṭi*), the jeweled fillet, and the *kramaśīrṣaka* should likewise be one sixteenth part each. The *āsārā*, however, consists of nine threads, and each is considered to be a basic unit (*mātṛka*).
The so-called Dharma-wheel is three units in measure and is situated upon a lotus seat.
The deer-band is also three units in measure according to its width and circumference;
the door should extend from the archway all around, including the mother-goddesses.
The row of petals of the universal lotus, beginning with the filaments, consists of three measures;
the vajra-garland should consist of three measures, and the auspicious radiance consists of six measures.
At the ends of the outward-facing treads, a vajra three measures high is raised.
Furthermore, it should hang down twelve *mātrās* in length.
The *ārā* spokes should be fashioned for the universal seat (*viśvāsana*) according to the divisions of the *āsārā* and so forth.
The corner-thread (*koṇasūtraka*), topped with bells and banners, should be six *mātrās* long.
"One should adorn the ground with blue powder, flowers, and so forth.
Thus it is said; [the mandala] has three times the length [of the door], with arches (toraṇa) possessing qualities such as the doors.
By means of the division of eight doors, there is the placement of an arch in the center.
The outer area should be twice the size of the inner sanctum, and the *ālaya* three times the size of the wheel (*cakra*).
Extending from the *ālaya*, the circular perimeter should be three times that size;
one who knows the logic of yoga should construct the mandala again according to the scriptures.
Thus concludes the introduction to the Tippa-sūtra-lopa. || 0 ||
In the east, there is a gateway beautifully adorned, named Jayamaṅgala;
then, one skilled in the maṇḍala of the Saṃgha should draw the emblem upon a lotus.
In the south, there is a gateway called Siddhighora, and there, upon a lotus, [one should likewise draw the emblem].
Furthermore, one should place the sign of a crocodile at the western gate;
there, in the lotus known as Vijayakarṣa,
one should install a banner that is exceedingly pure, specifically the one called Haṃsa.
In the north, the adept should likewise place the sign of a peacock upon a lotus for accomplishment and supernatural power; below that, moreover, is the Wheel of Dharma.
Then the teacher rises again, having offered the counter-oblation with flowers, incense, and so forth; he should speak thus, without a doubt.
Thus:
"Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life as well;
I shall undoubtedly become equal to the gods of the Samayas. [4.164+]
"Today is indeed my auspicious day; today my sacrifice is unsurpassed.
O Protector, out of compassion for all Buddhas, I carry out your command. Having recited this:
And with "new" [thread], there is the dyeing of five [threads] with five colors;
and that thread, consisting of gnosis, is again twice the length of the maṇḍala.
Therefore, the portion for the door is considered to be one-twentieth in thickness;
with that [portion],
smeared with the five nectars, it should be placed in the center of the hollowed palms.
One should draw the lines after having carefully inspected them from the perspective of the nature of the five Buddhas;
then, by means of the five-syllable mantra through the application of Vajrasattva.
Oṃ a ā aṃ āḥ.
The mantra for sprinkling the thread: || o ||
The Guru, having taken him aside to a secluded place, and the disciple likewise in that secluded place, says:
"O Blessed One, you who possess the eternal vajra, please grant me the sūtra.
All phenomena are mutually interpenetrating.
All phenomena follow one another; all phenomena have entered into one another utterly.
While the disciple, who destroys obstacles, recites "Ācārya" in this manner,
the teacher should cause the turning of that thread three times.
Then the disciple, having offered the flower of homage (*ātapuṣpa*), should recite the *trijaḥkāra*:
*jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ*.
Having grasped it with the left fist and held it at the center of the navel,
the preceptor then standing to the west and the disciple standing at the eastern door should indeed cast the knowledge-thread according to the sequence of clockwise rotation.
Oṃ, do not transgress the vajra-line; this is the time for you to act for the sake of sentient beings.
Having recited this mantra, one should place two lines in the sky.
The sequence for laying out the lines is now described. || 4.172+ || O ||

Having stepped upon the lords of the directions—Nāga and Indra, Yama and Yakṣa, Śikhin and Hara, Diś and Marut, Rakṣas and Vāteśa, Śikhin and Rākṣasa, Śikhin and Nabhasvant, and Bala and Īśvara—in a clockwise direction while facing them, excluding the northeast (Īśāna), the venerable Jñānasūtra, authorized by both teacher and disciple, is established in sequence around the hub of the wheel.
Thus, having doubled that very thread of knowledge, the true guru,
having placed that thread in the center according to the divisions beginning with Īśāna,
should cause the students to cast it by circling toward the right.

Having likewise fixed the inner thread, terrifying with a wrathful gaze, one should cast the *jñānasūtra* upon all the threads as before. Then, acting with majesty, the adept should burst open the four doors.
And so it is said in the *Rativajra*:
"In that regard, the Vajrācārya, remaining in the center and composed in meditative absorption..."
One should cause the four vajra-doors to spring open;
having cast them into the expanse of space, one should mentally open them according to their divisions in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should release that very thread of gnosis with the syllable *muḥ*.
This is the sequence of the thread of gnosis. || 4.177+ || o ||
Indeed, the powders placed within the individual vessels that have been prepared are truly fivefold,
consisting of gold in the forms of Vairocana and the other [Tathāgatas].
Then, having drawn the Tathāgatas into those [mandalas] that have been fumigated,
and having entered [them], preceded by the recitation of the offerings of water for the feet, water for sipping, and so forth,
one should transform [the deities] and contemplate them as abiding in the form of the *rajas* (powder).
Then the wise one, the wielder of the vajra, should address them with this mantra:
OṂ VAJRACITTASAMAYA HŪṂ.
Having lifted the wisdom-thread situated upon the wheel into the expanse of space, [he should proceed].
Having uttered the mantra "Vajravega," one should enter within:
"This is the pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), which liberates the realm of sentient beings;
we ourselves are the King Vajradhara, all the Tathāgatas."
For the sake of sentient beings, one should draw the wheel; may the Leaders consecrate it.
Having recited this statement, one should take recourse in the northeastern direction.
Having indeed grasped the particles with the left fist, one should proceed by taking them one particle at a time,
forming a circle that is free from the defects of being too tight, too loose, too thick, or too thin.
One should draw five lines, endowed with auspicious marks and pleasing to the mind;
having recited the mantra just mentioned, being composed in meditation,
one should delineate them in sequence using white, yellow, turmeric-red, and blue pigments.
This has been stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:

One needle is made of white vajra, another is golden and hanging; one needle is made of ruby, and another likewise of emerald. These should be known as black as well; this is considered the sequence of colors.
Having raised the line, they both exit out of fear of violating the covenant.
The mantra-practitioner, together with his disciple, should recite the *vajravega* mantra;
thereafter, the disciple should cause the artisan to apply the colored powders (*rajas*).
Having beheld the body of the Tathāgata, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, situated within the faces of the deities at the beginning.
Having indeed cast fragrant flowers into the region of the sky,
one should then perform a prostration according to the rule, with the knees touching the ground.
Having offered the water for honor, the water for the feet, and so forth, with a mind free from conceptual construction,
the mantra-practitioner, being fully concentrated, should recite this mantra three times.
Established in the pledge (*samaya*), thinking "You are the pledge, you are the pledge,
I am [the pledge]," one should then behold the Knowledge Being (*jñānasattva*) and the wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*) in the expanse of the sky;
having offered the water for the guest (*argha*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, one should cause them to enter into the image and other such objects.
First, one who possesses auspicious conduct and is skilled in mantras should smear a mirror with fragrant oil amidst the auspicious clamor of women.
The mantra of the taila [offering].
Oṃ, purification of the bodies of all Tathāgatas, svāhā!
One should smear [the vessel] with these five types of bark— derived from the *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *parkaṭī*, and *cūta*— placed within a bronze (*kāṃsa*) vessel.
Then, having smeared [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should bathe it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with the previously mentioned jars filled with pure water for the purpose of bathing.
First with the Vijaya-kumbha, then with the four families,
along with the family-mantras and family-vidyās of the Kuleśas who perform all rites.
With thirty-two jars and likewise with songs, musical instruments, and so forth,
one should daily recite the bathing verse impelled by all the Buddhas.
Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth,
so shall I bathe you with pure, divine water.
Oṃ, to the glory of the samaya of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ!
The wise know that for objects that are fashioned or cast, the bath is performed in this manner;
for variegated objects, they say it is done with a mirror, and especially for books.
Having lifted [the vessel] with a soft and clean cloth,
one should offer water and cover the face of the image with a yellow cloth.
Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite again with white mustard seeds and neem leaves,
one should likewise cast the white mustard seeds into the fire and then into the water while reciting the mantra.
Oṃ, to the vajra that burns all sins, burn all sin, svāhā!

Then, having sprinkled [the image] with water, one should worship it on all sides with flowers, incense, and other offerings, accompanied by songs and instrumental music, according to the sequence of the *vāribhakta-jaḍī* rite.
Holding the incense burner without distraction and placing one knee upon the ground,
one should recite the verses proclaimed by the Buddha while contemplating their meaning.
Just as all the perfectly awakened ones reside in Tuṣita,
and just as [the Buddha] dwelt in the womb of Queen Māyā, so too do you abide here in this form.
Remaining here perpetually as my protector, accept this worship and so forth for the sake of protection and for the increase of the spirit of awakening (bodhicitta).
Immediately thereafter,
having meditated upon the body as perfectly pure and endowed with the excellence of all aspects,
one should consecrate that body, speech, and mind with the three principles (tritatva).
Having placed the syllable Oṃ on the head, the syllable Āḥ in the region of the throat,
and having meditated on the syllable Hūṃ at the heart, one performs the purification of body, speech, and mind.
The Ritual for the Consecration of the Deity.
Thereafter, on another day, one with a virtuous mind should indeed perform a bath;
having shaken off the water with cloths or wiped it away with the hand, the wise one [should proceed].
Having removed [the old cloth],
one should then give that painting to be worn, having specially purified it with saffron and other substances,
as well as fine garments, perfumes, and so forth, consecrated by mantra.
Oṃ vajravāsase svāhā | Oṃ vajragandhe svāhā | Oṃ vajrābharaṇabhūṣaṇe svāhā |
Oṃ, divine food, that which gladdens through meditative absorption and contemplation, svāhā! Thereafter, the wise one should cause the excellent pledge to be heard, as impelled by the mantra.
Otherwise, it would undoubtedly result in harm for those who possess images and the like.
Oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ.
Herein is the hearing of the pledge (samaya).
Regarding "food":
one should offer flowers, sacrificial oblations, incense, lamps, betel,
or any other kind of substance, having consecrated it with mantras.
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe svāhā | Oṃ vajradhūpe svāhā | In this manner and so forth, one should present the offerings.

The fire-offering ritual (homakarma) as it has been prescribed therein must be performed by the practitioner; however, because it consists of many things that would require explanation, it has not been set forth here at present.
Having prepared the *caru* oblation, he should offer it to him with the recitation of mantras,
using honey contained in a silver vessel and [offering] with a golden probe.
He should open their eyes, whereby the vajra-eye is established;
the mantra-practitioner, being composed, should perform the consecration of the sense faculties and so forth.
Oṃ, to the eye, the purifier of the universal eye, svāhā!
One should visualize Kṣitigarbha in the eyes, Vajrapāṇi in the two ears,
Khagarbha in the nose, and Lokeśa in the region of the mouth.
One should meditate on Niṣkambhin in the heart and Samantabhadra in the body;
thereafter, one is the glorious Ghaṇṭādhara, intent upon brandishing the vajra.
The surface of the sky was completely filled by Vīṇādī, Locanā, and the others;
it was delightful with great clamor and adorned with the sound of kettledrums.
Having observed the wonderful musical performance filled with words of auspiciousness,
one should ring the bell and produce the most excellent sound of auspiciousness.
Lakṣmīdhara, who resembles a mountain of gold, the lord of the three worlds, free from the three impurities,
the Buddha with eyes like the petals of a blossomed lotus— may he bring you the triple auspiciousness and peace today.
Thus instructed was the preeminent one, unshakable, renowned throughout the three worlds, and honored by men and gods;
he is the supreme Dharma, the bringer of peace to all beings—may he be for you the second auspicious blessing in this world.

Endowed with the true Dharma, rich in auspiciousness and virtue, the Saṅgha is worthy of offerings from humans, gods, and asuras; abiding in modesty and glory, the most excellent among assemblies, may it be for you the third auspicious blessing in this world.

Whatever auspiciousness there was when the Tathāgata descended here from the womb of the Tuṣita celestial palace for the benefit of the world, followed by the gods including Indra— may that auspiciousness bring you peace today.

May that auspiciousness which occurred at the birth of the Lord, the ender of existence, in the delightful Lumbinī grove— adorned with shoots and radiant blossoms, and nourished by many gods— be a source of peace for you today.

May that auspiciousness which attended the Tathāgata as he proceeded through the forest of asceticism at midnight with joy, followed by yakṣas and gods for the sake of destroying manifold sufferings— may that auspiciousness bring you peace today.
Whatever auspiciousness there was in the preeminent city called Kapila, which was praised by the high-souled gods beginning with Acyuta,
and which belonged to the Tathāgata of infinite virtue— may that auspiciousness bring you peace today.

Whatever auspiciousness belongs to him whose body is like blazing gold, who rests upon a bed of grass the color of beryl, and who remains perfectly motionless in the firmest of cross-legged postures— may that auspiciousness bring peace to you today.
Whatever auspiciousness there was when the Teacher, the Sugata, while proclaiming the excellent Wheel of Dharma and staying at Vārāṇasī,
became manifest as a great wonder upon the earth and in the sky— may that auspiciousness bring you peace today.

Whatever auspiciousness is beneficial, supreme, pure, a source of meritorious action, and cherished by noble beings— may all that which the Blessed One, the Sage Śākyasiṃha, proclaimed for the entire world, be today an auspicious bringer of peace for you.
This, moreover, should be recited at the time of the formal acceptance (adhivāsana) and so forth.
Having performed it in this manner, the lord of yogins, being composed, should question the disciple.
"That which was requested by you for the purpose of properly establishing [the image] has indeed been completed;
now perform the worship as you please."
Oṃ supratiṣṭhitavajre svāhā.
Having offered flowers, incense, and so forth, and again with the clamor of musical instruments,
one should dissolve the maṇḍala after asking for forgiveness, using the language of the mantra.
May the perfectly awakened ones, the deities together with their sons, the hosts of gods beginning with the Buddha, and especially the world-protectors, themselves grant forgiveness.
Having established well-being and peace everywhere for me, the donor,
may they always provide protection for immeasurable sentient beings.
The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished for you, and success has been granted according to your needs.
Go now to the realm of the Buddhas, and return once more.
May earth, fire, water, and air provide such protection that one's fame may endure for a long time— whether for an eon or even for a hundred eons.
And may the pleased deities return once more to their own auspicious abode;
may they protect my sons, grandsons, and others, and grant happiness to me, the donor.
Having thus dedicated the merit even of the donor toward enlightenment, one should perform the rite of dismissal while ringing the bell with a solemn flourish. ||o||
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for consecration.
